The other words (hallucination, talons, solstice, sarcastic, juvenile) are taught through context and the glossary or a dictionary. Word parts taught: un- (not), -er (person who), -ance / -ness idea (state of), dis- (opposite/away) with courage, and -ent / -s (plural people)."},{"type":"teach","move":"teach","text":"Show *unusual*. Underline un-. Say: un- means not, and usual means ordinary. So unusual means not ordinary. Find it on p. 17 and read the sentence around it."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Using un- and what you know about usual, what does unusual mean? What other un- words do you know?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Unusual means not normal or strange. Other words are unhappy, unfair, and unlikely."},{"type":"teach","move":"teach","text":"Show *eavesdropper* (p. 19). Circle -er, which means a person who does something. Explain that eavesdrop means to listen in secretly, so an eavesdropper is a person who secretly listens. Have students find the sentence on p. 19 and decide who is being called one."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What does the -er ending tell us about this word? What are other words that name a person with -er?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"It tells us the word names a person who does the action. Like teacher, swimmer, and baker. An eavesdropper is a person who listens in on private talk."},{"type":"teach","move":"teach","text":"Show *ignorance* (p. 19) and *discouraged* (p. 21). Ignorance comes from ignore/ignorant and the ending -ance names a state: the state of not knowing. In discouraged, dis- means taking away and courage means bravery, so discouraged means having courage taken away. The -ed ending shows it describes how someone feels."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What is left when you take courage away? How would a discouraged student act on a field trip?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"You are left feeling like you can't do it. A discouraged student might be quiet, give up, or act like he doesn't care."},{"type":"teach","move":"teach","text":"Show *delinquents* (p. 22) and *juvenile* (p. 22). Together they appear in the phrase juvenile delinquents. Juvenile means young. Delinquents are young people who break rules. Have students use context on p. 22 to explain what kind of label this is and how Percy might feel being called one."},{"type":"directions","text":"Open your Personal Dictionary. For *unusual*, *eavesdropper*, and *discouraged*, underline the base word, circle the prefix or suffix, and write the meaning in your own words. Then use a dictionary or glossary to check the meaning and part of speech of *solstice* and *sarcastic*."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Help English learners use word parts and a reference source to figure out meaning, building toward reading closely.","sayAsk":"Say each word aloud with a partner and clap the syllables. An inference is a conclusion we draw from clues. Strong readers cite the exact words for both."},{"type":"directions","text":"Reread pp. 16–22. Make a three-column chart: Character or moment (Percy, Grover, Mr. Brunner), What the text says (explicit, with a short quote and page), What it hints at (your inference). Add at least one row for each of the three."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"I will model one. On p. 16, Percy is shaken by something he sees and the text uses the word hallucination to describe what he thinks it was. Explicitly, he is trying to explain away something strange. It hints that what he saw was real, because the danger keeps returning."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What details show Percy's behavior at the museum? What does the narrator's voice tell us about how he sees himself?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Percy tries to stay out of trouble but still gets into trouble. His narration is honest and kind of joking, and he seems to expect that people will blame him. That hints he has a reason to be nervous, because strange things follow him."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What does Grover's nervousness show? Which words or actions tell you?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Grover acts jumpy and worried and keeps watching Percy and the teacher. That hints that Grover knows more than he is saying and is trying to protect Percy."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What does Mr. Brunner's lecture say explicitly, and what is hinted at by his teaching on p. 19 and what he says about the gods and the solstice?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Explicitly, he is teaching about Greek mythology and the gods and what ancient people believed. It hints that these old stories matter more than a school subject, and that he is warning or testing Percy, because the details match what Percy has been experiencing."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"How does the author's word choice, like talons, ignorance, or sarcastic, affect the tone?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Talons sounds scary and animal-like, so it makes the mood dangerous. Sarcastic shows tension between Percy and the adults. The words together make the tone nervous and suspicious."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Support students in reading closely and explaining how a writer's word choices point to hidden meaning.","sayAsk":"Say: Show me the exact words. Ask: What does the text say? What do you think it hints at? Frames: The text says ___ on page ___. This suggests ___ because ___. The word ___ makes the scene feel ___. Expand sentences with adverbials: Grover looked nervously at Percy during the lecture.","watchFor":"If students retell without quoting, then prompt: Which words prove that? Success: students pair a quote with an inference and an adverbial detail."},{"type":"pulse-check","standards":["RL.6.1"],"stem":"Which statement best shows an inference, rather than an explicit detail, about the museum trip?","choices":[{"text":"Mr. Brunner leads a lecture about Greek mythology at the museum.","correct":false,"rationale":"This is stated directly in the text, so it is an explicit detail, not an inference."},{"text":"Grover acts nervous around Percy, which hints that he knows about a danger Percy does not yet understand.","correct":true,"rationale":"It uses a stated behavior and draws a conclusion beyond the words on the page, which is an inference."},{"text":"The class goes to a museum on a field trip.","correct":false,"rationale":"The text states this plainly, so it is explicit."},{"type":"x","text":"Percy is a student in Mr. Brunner's class.","correct":false,"rationale":"This is a stated fact about the character, not an inference."}]},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: telling explicit from inferred","tryThis":"Give two columns labeled I can point to it and I figured it out. Have students place each detail in one column and underline the words that prove it."},{"situation":"Ready for extension","tryThis":"Ask students to find a moment where Percy's narration (point of view) makes the danger seem funny or ordinary, and explain how that choice affects suspense."}]}]},{"id":"lia-rising-action","title":"Part B: How the Museum Scene Builds the Plot","minutes":15,"standards":["RL.6.1","RL.6.3","RL.6.5","L.6.5"],"routine":"Quick Write","blocks":[{"type":"text-reference","title":"The Lightning Thief","pages":"pp. 16–22"},{"type":"teach","move":"teach","text":"Rising action is the part of a plot where events build tension. Each scene adds pressure. Authors layer in new information and warning signs so the later confrontation feels earned, not random."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Think of the museum as a step on a staircase. Chapter 1 started the climb, and this chapter takes us higher by adding mythology and danger signs."},{"type":"directions","text":"Add two columns to your notes: Mythology content (what we learn about the Greek gods and myths) and Danger signs (what warns us trouble is coming). Fill in at least two details in each, with page numbers."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What mythology content does the museum scene add to the story? What danger signs does it plant?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"The lecture adds stories about Greek gods and monsters. The danger signs are Percy's strange vision, Grover's nervousness, and the way adults treat Percy like a troublemaker. Together they warn us that something bigger will happen."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"How does the museum field trip reveal fears and values about ancient powers still being present in the modern world?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"The trip shows that people, like Grover and Mr. Brunner, take old myths seriously and fear that those powers are still around, even though most adults call it just a story. The museum is a modern place full of ancient things, so it shows that the past and present are mixed together."},{"type":"directions","text":"Quick Write (4–5 sentences): Explain how the museum field trip fits into the plot as rising action. Use at least two cited details, one from Percy, Grover, or Mr. Brunner, and the transition words *for example*, *this suggests*, or *as a result*. Add at least two adverbials (when, where, how, or why)."},{"type":"paragraph","audience":"teacher","text":"Model starter: In Chapter 2, the museum field trip works as rising action because it adds mythology and warning signs that build tension. For example, Grover acts nervously during the lecture, which suggests he is hiding something. As a result, readers expect a larger confrontation later in the story."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Support students in explaining a scene's role in the plot and adding precise details with adverbials.","sayAsk":"Say: Add where, when, how, or why to your sentence. Ask: What does this scene add to the story? Frames: The museum scene is rising action because ___. For example, ___ (page ___). This builds toward ___. Grover spoke quietly in the museum because ___.","watchFor":"If students only summarize the scene, then prompt: How does it make the story more tense? If students skip a quote, then ask: Which words show that? Success: students link a cited detail to rising action and use at least one adverbial."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: connecting a scene to the larger plot","tryThis":"Provide the frame: In this scene, ___ happens. It adds ___, so later ___ could happen. Let students say it to a partner before writing."},{"situation":"Ready for extension","tryThis":"Ask students to predict one later confrontation and explain which two details from today most clearly foreshadow it."}]}]}]},{"kind":"look-back","title":"Look Back","purpose":"Students check their understanding of how details build the plot and reflect on the strategies that helped.","activities":[{"id":"look-back-reflect","title":"Complete the Claim","minutes":5,"standards":["RL.6.1","RL.6.5"],"routine":"Reflection","blocks":[{"type":"paragraph","audience":"shared","text":"In the Performance Task, you will explain how scenes contribute to a story's plot. One detail that proves it is ___ (page ___). This detail suggests ___."},{"type":"sample-response","text":"The museum field trip is important to the plot because it adds Greek mythology and danger signs that build tension. One detail that proves it is that Grover acts nervous during the lecture (page 19). This detail suggests he knows something is wrong and is protecting Percy."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Collect responses as an exit check.
